lines.text: [warm] Helm to all stations, and a word before we move, because this is not how a run starts. Every corridor you have flown so far had a roof and a floor and two walls. In four seconds the walls of this one go to nothing, and they do not come back. Taking them down now.

[hushed] Walls at half. Quarter. Gone — and there is ground out there. Ridges away to port, a summit standing well off the bow, and the rail we are riding is running along the floor of a valley I did not know we were in. Turn your head. Nobody is going to talk for a moment.

[dry] That is the first time on any of these runs that I have been able to see past the paintwork. Doc, what am I actually looking at? Because it looks like country, and country is not what I understood I was signing up for on a mathematics tour.

[gentle] It is country, and it is a function. Every place on the flat ground below us has an address — two numbers, how far across and how far along. The rule takes those two numbers and hands back exactly one: a height. That is all a landscape is.

[dry] Helm has beads to drop over the side and I want you ahead of him for once. A bead falls, it finds the flat ground, and then what does it do — sit there, or something else? Commit to an answer in your head before they go. You only get to be wrong about this once.

[reflective] Forty beads away. They found the floor, every one of them, and then they stood up — each one to its own height and no two the same. All the tall ones are clustered off to port under that summit, and the short ones are out in the bowl to starboard.

[warm] That rise is the rule being asked and the rule answering. Each bead read its address off the flat ground first, then went to the one height that address is worth. That was not decoration. You watched a surface being sampled into existence, one place at a time.

[reflective] And it holds still. Doc, if I turn my head the mountain stays exactly where it was, off the port bow, at the same distance, the same size. It is not painted on the window and it is not following me about. It is out there, and we are down inside it.

[gentle] It holds still, which is what open ground does. Until today the passage was one number going in and one coming out, and we could hang the whole of it above the rail. From here it is two going in — and the input has stopped being a number. It is a place to stand.

[reflective] Two in, one out. So that roof I have been reading all the way here was only ever the special case where I was not allowed to turn left. Nobody mentioned there was a left, or that the corridor had been standing in the middle of something the whole time.

[warm] Then that is the stop, and it is one sentence long. One number handed back for every place on the ground, and what you get is a country you can fly. Say that back in your own words, out loud to the window if you like, and if it comes out whole we can move.

transitLines.text: [warm] Under way along the valley floor, walls staying down for the duration. Doc wants to cut this country in two directions at once, which he assures me is easier than it sounds, and I have learned not to argue with him before the second stop.

lines.text: [gentle] Glass in a moment. First, back to the beads: each one had to read something off the flat ground before it knew how high to stand. What did it read, and how many numbers was that? Work it out in your own head. I am not going to say it for you.

[warm] Holding station. Two great sheets of glass standing straight through the hull, one running fore and aft, one running port to starboard. Where each sheet meets the ground there is a bright line being drawn along it, and the two lines cross underneath us.

[gentle] Look at one sheet only, and ignore the rest of the country. Along that sheet your side-to-side position never changes — it is pinned. So the ground under it is a single curve with a single input, and that is the thing we took the closing jaws to, run after run.

[dry] Then you have cheated, Doc. You have gone to the trouble of opening the walls and giving me a whole country, and the first thing you have done is slice it until it is a corridor again. Two corridors, if I count the glass properly, but corridors all the same.

[warm] I have, and it is the trick of the entire run, and it is not cheating because I intend to do it in every direction before we are done. Arms out, Helm. One jaw into each sheet, and take me a tangent needle off each of those two curves.

[dry] Hold on. Before he pulls them — two needles, one for each direction, off one spot on one hillside. Are they coming up at the same tilt or not? Pick one. I have picked mine and I will tell you afterwards whether I turned out to be any good at this.

[reflective] Both jaws on. Port needle is tilted up, call it fifteen degrees. Forward needle is tilted down. Doc, they disagree with each other — and we are one ship, sitting in one place, on one piece of ground, and I have not moved a metre.

[dry] I said the same tilt. I said it out loud, and I was wrong inside four seconds, which is a personal record even for me. One ship, one spot, one piece of dirt, and the ground cannot make up its mind what it is doing underneath us.

[grave] That disagreement is the whole concept and it is a metre in front of your face. At this one spot the ground climbs if you go left and falls if you go straight on. There is no such thing as the slope here. There is a slope for each direction you pick.

[gentle] Each of those needles has a name — a partial derivative. Partial, because it only answers about one direction and holds the other one still. Nothing new was invented for it. It is the same measurement as before, taken twice, along two cuts.

[warm] So the sentence to carry out is this. Hold one direction still and you are back to a single curve you already know how to handle, and there is one of those for every direction you might choose. Say it back in your own words and this stop is finished.

transitLines.text: [warm] Hold those two needles in your head while we move. At the next stop we put something on top of them, and the question is whether they will take the weight. If they do, a great deal of what follows gets straightforward. If they do not, we will say so.

lines.text: [gentle] We left the last stop carrying two of something, one off each arm. What were they, and what was the single question that each one of them answered? Get that straight before you look down, because the whole of this stop is about to be balanced on top of them.

[warm] Plate is coming down. Square, rigid, four units on a side, and it is settling onto the two needles we cut at the last stop. One point of contact, one tilt each way, and it has stopped moving. It is held there. It is not resting on the ground at all.

[gentle] Two needles are enough to fix a flat sheet completely. Give me a point to pass through, a tilt one way and a tilt the other, and there is exactly one flat surface in the world that agrees with all three. That plate is not a guess. It is the only answer.

[dry] It is held on the needles and it is nowhere near the ground. There is a gap under the far corner the size of my arm, out where the country starts bending away from us. That plate is a poor description of this hillside and I want that on the record.

[warm] There is a gap, and I have coloured it in so you can see the exact size of your complaint. That film is the difference between the flat sheet and the real ground. Keep your eye on the far corner and not on the middle. The middle has nothing to show you.

[dry] And before Helm moves — he is about to fly us in close, twice over. That coloured film out under the far corner: does it get thinner, does it stay exactly as it is, or does it thicken up? One of the three, chosen now. I have chosen and I am not saying.

[reflective] Inflating. The ridges are opening out and going lazy. Again — and the film under the plate is thinning. It has gone from an arm's width to a coat of paint, and the plate and the ground are reading as one object from where I sit.

[dry] Doc, I have to say it. You zoomed in. Of course it looks flat. If I put my eye against a barrel it looks flat too, and the barrel is still a barrel and my beer still runs out of the end of it. You have shown me nothing about the ground. You have shown me how close we are standing.

[grave] You are right, and I am glad you said it out loud, because that is the honest shape of this. The ground is not becoming flat. It is doing precisely what it always did. The thing that is changing is us, and how much we can still tell apart from in here.

[gentle] The real claim is smaller than the picture and stronger. It is this: the gap shrinks faster than the distance you walked to open it. Walk half as far and the error is less than half. That plate has a name, the tangent plane, and that promise is what earns it.

[reflective] So the plate is not a description of the country. It is a promise about how fast the country leaves it, and the terms are that the gap dies quicker than the walk that opened it. Say that much back in your own words and I am content, and so is he.

[gentle] Drum in a moment. First: the plate made you a promise back there, and the promise had a size to it. What was being promised, and what had to happen to that coloured film for the promise to hold? Answer it to yourself. This whole stop leans on it.

[warm] Belly drum is deployed and reading. It has put an arrow out at our position — bright, about two units long — and it swings as we move. At this instant it is pointing off to port and a little forward, at the shoulder of that summit off the bow.

[dry] Stop there. Doc is about to tell us what that arrow is, and everybody already knows it points uphill. So point at where you think it is lying. Up on the hillside, tipped along the slope — or flat on the ground like a compass needle? Choose before he opens his mouth.

[gentle] Now look at it properly, because this is the one thing almost every book draws loosely. It is lying flat on the ground. It is not on the hillside. It does not tilt up the slope by so much as a degree — and if you said it did, you are in very large company.

[dry] Then it is pointing at the dirt, Doc. You have just told me that the uphill arrow does not point uphill. Say that again slowly and say it to my face, because from where I am standing it looks like you have dropped one somewhere and not noticed.

[warm] You are right to hold me to it. It is a direction to walk, not a direction to climb. It answers one question: standing here, which way do I set off across the flat map to gain height fastest? The answer to that is a bearing, and a bearing lies flat.

[gentle] And it carries a second thing in its length: how steeply the ground rises if you do walk that way. For the next stretch watch the length alone and never mind where it is pointing. Helm, take us over the shoulder, and then down into the bowl to starboard.

[reflective] Over the shoulder it was long and hard. Out here in the bowl it is a stub — down to about a fifth of a unit, and swinging about as though it cannot make up its mind which way to face. The ground under us is very nearly level and the drum knows it.

[warm] Which is right, and honest. On level ground there is no best way to set off, so the arrow has almost nothing to say and it says almost nothing. Helm, drop a heavy bead on the shoulder. And you call this one: which way does it run, and how near the arrow?

[reflective] Bead released and running. It is away downhill and leaving a bright track behind it — and Doc, it is running dead against the arrow. Not near it. Not roughly. Along the same line, backwards, as though somebody had laid a rail down for it.

[grave] Every time, wherever we drop it, and that arrow is built out of the two needles from the last stop laid flat and added as bearings. So: the uphill arrow lies on the ground, it points the way to walk, and its length is how steep that walk will be. Say it back.

transitLines.text: [dry] A direction to walk, not a direction to climb. I have written that on the back of my hand, which is where I put things I intend to say to people at parties. It is the first entry on there in about five years that I actually understand.

lines.text: [gentle] Rings on the ground in a moment. First, the arrow we have just spent so long on. Where does it lie, and what does its length tell you that its direction does not? Two separate answers to that. Have them both before Helm starts turning us.

[warm] The country has come up in rings. Twelve of them, drawn on the ground like tide marks left on a beach, and I am putting us on one and following it. Course is going to wander badly — this line bends all over the place and I am not fighting it.

[gentle] Let it wander. Every place on the ring you are on has the same height as every other. That is all a contour is: a walk on which you never gain and never lose. A map maker draws them; a tired hill walker follows them and keeps his legs.

[dry] Before she takes the first bend — the arrow is out over the nose right now. When she hauls round to port and follows that ring, what does the arrow do? Swings round with her, stays where it is pointing, or something I have not thought of? Say it before it happens.

[reflective] Hard to port. Arrow swung with me and it is still square across the bow. Coming right, thirty degrees — still square. Doc, it is welded at a right angle to my heading and I promise you on the log that I am not steering the thing.

[warm] Keep your eye on it for the whole of this leg, because I am not going to assert this one at you. I would rather you got bored of watching it be true. Helm, take every bend the ring gives you and do not straighten out for anything.

[gentle] Nobody is steering it. It falls straight out of what the two words mean. Along the ring you gain no height whatsoever, so that heading has no climbing in it at all — and the fastest climb has to be the one direction with none of the ring in it.

[dry] The rings ahead are packed in tight. Four or five almost touching, all the way over that shoulder, and then out to starboard they are spread so wide I can barely find the next one. Same country, same rings, and they cannot agree how far apart to stand.

[warm] Then watch the arrow's length as Helm crosses the packed set, and watch it again out where they lie wide apart. Crowded rings mean a lot of height gained in a very short walk. The map is telling you the steepness without printing a single number on itself.

[reflective] It doubled going through the packed ones and out in the spread it is the stub again. I have read a hundred walking maps and never once understood that the crowding was the information. Walk a ring and you never climb, and the arrow is always square to the walk. Say that back and it is yours.

[gentle] Dial coming down. Before it does: on the ring you followed, what was the angle between your heading and the arrow, and why did it have to be that and nothing else? Say the reason to yourself, not just the number. Then we lay sixteen headings out at once.

[warm] Dial is down. Sixteen spokes lying flat on the ground all round the ship, evenly spaced, with a needle standing up at the end of each one. They are all at different tilts. I am going to yaw us slowly through the whole ring so you get each in turn.

[gentle] Each needle answers one question: if I set off along this spoke, how steeply does the ground climb? Sixteen headings, sixteen answers. Two of them you have already met — the fore-and-aft one and the port-and-starboard one are the needles from the two sheets.

[dry] Before she yaws us anywhere — the tips of those sixteen needles are going to trace out a shape. Draw it in your head now. Is it a circle or is it not? And if it is not, where is the longest needle of the lot going to be lying? Commit to both before she turns.

[dry] I said circle. It is not a circle. Run your eye round the tips and it is a fat lobe out one side and a dent on the other, and the longest needle in the set is lying along something I recognise. Doc, tell me it is lying where I think it is lying.

[warm] It is lying exactly along the compass arrow, and that is what fastest meant. Out of every heading available to you at this spot, nothing climbs harder than that one. Now watch the needle that stands square to it as Helm brings us round to port.

[reflective] Coming round to port. Needles falling away as I turn. Passing the one that sits square to the arrow now — and that needle is flat. Dead flat. No tilt in it at all, and I am holding us here so that everybody gets a proper look at it.

[gentle] Which is the contour, come back to see you. Past it the needles drop below flat and the lobe turns into that dent, because those headings are downhill — and the deepest of them is lying straight against the arrow, exactly where the bead ran.

[dry] So sixteen separate measurements, and every one of them was already sitting inside that one arrow before you laid the dial down? Then why lay the dial down at all? I am not complaining. I would like to know when I am being shown a thing and when I am being shown a proof.

[warm] To find out that they were. Take the arrow, take your heading, and the steepness you actually feel is the arrow's shadow cast along the way you are pointing. Full length when you face it, nothing at all when you stand across it, negative behind you.

[gentle] We used that word once before, back on the wheel where a spinning point threw a shadow that drew the wave. Same act here, new country. So: whatever heading you pick, the steepness you feel is the arrow's shadow on that heading. Say it back and we are done.

transitLines.text: [warm] Dial stowed. Climbing out of the bowl and heading for high ground — Doc has picked us a spot where the country apparently cannot make up its mind what it is. It is marked on the chart as a pass, and he says that is the polite name for it.

lines.text: [gentle] Before we park. On the dial, one needle came out perfectly flat. Which heading was that one, and what was true about the ground along it? Have your answer ready, because the place we are going is built out of flat needles and nothing else.

[warm] Parked in the middle of a pass. High ground rising away to port and to starboard, and the land falling off ahead of us and behind. The two cutting sheets are back up, and there is a curve on each of them crossing right underneath the hull.

[gentle] Look at the two curves and not at the scenery. The one running port to starboard arches up over the top of us — along that cut we are at the highest point there is. The one running fore and aft dips underneath us. Along that cut, we are at the lowest.

[dry] So we are on a summit and at the bottom of a valley at the same moment. Doc, that is not a place, that is a contradiction, and I would like to watch you get out of that one without moving the ship. One of those two curves has to be lying to me.

[warm] It is a place, and you have stood in one. It is a mountain pass — it is why a road over a range goes exactly where it goes, because the lowest way across is a high point of the ridge. Both statements are true because they answer two different questions.

[reflective] Both tangent needles are horizontal. Flat one way, flat the other way, and the belly drum is reading the compass arrow as nothing at all. There is no uphill from this spot, Doc. There is no downhill from it either, and that is a first.

[grave] And here is the trap. We have met flat ground before, back at the spot where the tilting stopped and we all quietly took it for the top. Flat only ever means the ground has stopped tilting. What kind of place it is has to be settled afterwards, by how the ground bends.

[gentle] Helm, a ball down at our feet. Then two nudges — one forward along the low cut, one to port along the high one. Before he touches either: does that ball come back to us, or is it gone? Answer for both nudges separately. Do not let me tell you.

[reflective] Ball down, and it sat there perfectly still. Nudged forward along the low cut: it ran away and it has not come back. Fresh ball, nudged to port: climbed a little, slowed, stopped, and rolled straight back down to us. Same place, two nudges.

[reflective] A place that holds if you push it one way and lets go if you push it the other. It has a name on a horse and I never once thought of a mountain as one. A summit one way and a valley the other, and it is a real kind of place. Say that back and we can leave.

[gentle] Before the clip goes on. At the pass both needles were flat and the arrow had nothing at all to say. What did that tell you about the place, and what did it completely fail to tell you? There are two parts to that. Take a moment over the second one.

[warm] Tether is on. There is a fence-line drawn across this country and we are clipped to it — I have steering along it, but I cannot leave it. Contour rings are lit up underneath us again, and the fence is cutting straight across them. Eight so far.

[gentle] This is the shape of nearly every real problem anyone is ever paid to solve. You want the highest ground you can reach, but you are not free to go and get it. There is a budget, a coastline, a road, a fixed length of wire. Here it is a fence, and you stay on it.

[dry] Then the summit is no use to me at all. It is a long way off this line and I cannot reach it, so what am I actually hunting for out here? The tallest place the fence happens to pass through, I suppose, but how would I know it when I got there?

[warm] Watch the rings as Helm rides forward and the fence will tell you itself. Every time it crosses a ring we have changed height. So as long as the fence is still cutting across contours, there is climbing left on this line and we are not there yet.

[reflective] Two arrows out now. The ground's uphill arrow, and a second one standing square to the fence itself. They are pointing in visibly different directions, call it forty degrees apart, and the crossing angle is flattening as we run.

[dry] Then it is going to run out of angle. Before it does — when the fence stops cutting rings and we are standing on the best point there is, what do those two arrows do? They are forty degrees apart as I speak. Say what you expect to be looking at, and then watch.

[hushed] The fence has stopped cutting the rings. It has come up against one of them and just grazed it — touched it and turned away without ever crossing over. And the two arrows have swung together. They are lying on top of each other, Doc. There is one arrow out there now.

[warm] That is the theorem, and it took two seconds. At the best point on the fence there is no climbing left along the fence, so the fence must be running along a contour there — and both arrows stand square to that same contour, which leaves them nowhere to be except in line.

[reflective] So I never go hunting for the answer itself. I hunt for the moment the two arrows agree, and that is a far cheaper thing to go looking for, especially along a fence a hundred miles long. Does it have a name, Doc, so I can find it in a book?

[gentle] It is Lagrange's method, and in a book it is three lines of symbols that give nobody the faintest idea what is going on. What is going on is this: the best point on a fence is where the fence just grazes a contour. Say that back and keep the picture.

transitLines.text: [warm] Tether released, back on open steering. Doc is asking me for level ground and a lot of room, because apparently we are about to grow a forest out of it. He has not said what kind of forest and I have stopped asking that sort of question.

lines.text: [gentle] Level ground, and it is about to sprout. Before it does: out on the fence, what was it you were actually hunting for, and why was that a cheaper hunt than looking for the answer itself? Say it to yourself. Then we stop climbing and start adding up.

[warm] The ground is growing columns. Square-sectioned, one for every cell of the grid, each rising until its top touches the country above it. Twelve by twelve of them, and I am taking us in between — the tops make a stepped version of the roof, so mind your head.

[gentle] We cut the space under a curve into standing slabs once and added them up. This is that same act with one more direction in it. Every column is a little tower of stuff: its base is one square of ground, its height is the country directly above that square.

[dry] And the tops are all wrong. They are flat and the country above them is not flat anywhere. Every single column is over or under by a shaving, and there are a hundred and forty-four of them out there making exactly the same mistake at once.

[warm] Every one, and that is honest arithmetic rather than a flaw — we know the error is there and we are about to go and kill it. The running bar on the deck is the total of all of them, and it is close already. Helm, halve the cell, and then halve it again.

[dry] Hold it, before she halves anything. Four times as many columns, each on a quarter of the footprint. Does that running bar leap, creep, or sit where it is? And are we killing the shavings faster than we are breeding columns? Call both, and then just watch.

[reflective] Halving. Four times the columns, a quarter of the footprint each. The steps have got shorter and the bar has moved — not by much. Halving again, and we are properly inside a forest now. Bar moved less that time than it did the first time.

[gentle] Watch the roof of the forest rather than the bar. It was a staircase; it is turning into the country itself. Each halving shrinks the shavings much faster than it multiplies the columns, and that is exactly why this settles down instead of running away from us.

[warm] And Helm's bar has stopped moving in the second figure. So we have the volume under this piece of country, and we got it by adding up towers. That is a double integral. There is nothing in it you did not do with the slabs — you have chopped the floor in both directions instead of one.

[reflective] Flying through it is what does it. Seen from above that is a graph in a textbook; from in here, with the columns going past on both sides, it is a warehouse and I am counting stock. The volume under a landscape is a floor of columns. Say that back and I will sit down.

[gentle] The forest is still standing. Before we cut it: what exactly was one column worth, and what did halving the cell do to the total on the deck? Both of those, in your own head. Nothing about the forest changes here. Only the way we walk through it.

[warm] Forest is still standing. I have a lit plane at the near edge and I am going to walk it the length of the field, fore to aft, harvesting whole rows of columns as it goes. Gold wake behind it, and the bar on the measuring deck climbing as it eats.

[gentle] So the order is this. Take one row of columns, add that row up to a single number, and then add all those row-totals together as the plane advances. Two additions, one sitting inside the other, and the outer one only ever sees the numbers the inner one handed it.

[reflective] Plane is through the far edge. Gold bar is standing at its full height on the deck and I am marking it. Resetting the field now — columns coming back up, wake cleared, bar held exactly where it is for the comparison.

[dry] And now you will do it sideways instead and tell me it comes out the same. I will take that bet, but I want it on record first that it does not look obvious to me. Those are two completely different piles of arithmetic and you know it.

[warm] It is not obvious, and you should hold on to that. Nothing in the second sweep visits the same columns in the same order or adds up the same running numbers along the way. Helm, take the blue plane across, port to starboard.

[dry] And before it moves, everybody call it. When that blue bar has finished climbing, is it shorter than the gold one, longer than it, or exactly level? Pick one and hold on to it. Nobody talk. I want to know whether I believed my own bet.

[reflective] Blue plane away. Harvesting columns instead of rows this time, and the blue bar climbed on a completely different schedule to the gold — behind it, then ahead of it, then behind again. Through the far side. Blue bar is up beside the gold.

[dry] They are the same length. Not close, Doc, the same, to the pixel, and I have moved my head twice to check it from another angle. I withdraw the objection and I am mildly annoyed about how quickly that happened.

[gentle] Because both sweeps ate exactly the same forest. Nothing was created by choosing a direction to walk in, and nothing was lost. The volume was standing there before either plane moved, and all the plane ever decided was the order of the adding.

[grave] One honest note. This is Fubini's theorem, and it has small print: for country like ours, no cliffs and no holes, the two orders always agree, and there are nastier objects where they do not. Row by row or column by column, the same total. Say it back.

transitLines.text: [dry] Nastier objects. Every time you say a thing like that and then fly straight past it, Doc, I put a tick in a notebook. There are four ticks in it now and we are only on the fifth run. One day somebody will have to fly me down that notebook.

lines.text: [gentle] Before the floor moves under you. The two sweeps came out level with each other — what was it about the forest itself that made that happen, before either plane took a step? One sentence, in your head, now, because I am about to break the thing it relied on.

[warm] The grid on the ground is coming loose. Straight lines bending — the whole floor is turning from squares into rings and spokes, and the country is riding along on top of it, unmoved. Five seconds. There. Completely different lines under the same landscape.

[gentle] Nothing about this country has changed. The hills are exactly where they were. What has changed is how we are addressing the ground: instead of how far across and how far along, it is now how far out and which way round. Same places, new names for them.

[dry] We did this once before, to the rings on the wall — re-spaced them until the numbers behaved, and not one thing that mattered moved an inch. What is different about doing it to the floor, other than making me feel slightly unwell about my footing?

[warm] For exactly that reason — some countries are far easier to add up in rings than in squares, and a good navigator picks his grid. But there is a bill this time, and the bill is the whole stop. Helm, light one cell and keep it lit wherever it goes.

[dry] Then before it goes anywhere. That lit patch of ground is four-sided and fat where it sits now. When Helm carries it inward through the warp, does it hold its size? Yes or no — and if no, which way? Keep your eye on the patch and on nothing else at all.

[reflective] Cell lit and carried inward through the warp. Doc, it is not holding its size. Out on the rim it was fat and square. In here it has gone to a sliver, thin as a blade, and the plates hanging off the bow are dropping right along with it.

[gentle] And that is the thing you must not lose. When the columns were standing, every one of them had the same footprint, so the total was simply heights added up. Bend the grid and the footprints stop being equal — and a tall column standing on a sliver is worth almost nothing.

[warm] So we carry a correction, and it is not an abstraction. There it is: two plates hanging off the bow. One is that cell before the bend, one is the same cell after it. Their ratio is the entire correction, measured live, and it changes as the cell moves.

[dry] So the bookkeeping for all of this is one area held against another area. That is a ratio I could measure myself with a tape and an afternoon, which is not what I expected from a stop you have been building up to since breakfast.

[gentle] It is, and that is the honest size of it. The number is called the Jacobian, and the machinery for computing it without a tape belongs to another expedition. Bend the grid and every little cell changes area by a factor you can measure. Say that back and we are finished.

[gentle] Before we slow down. On the bent ground, why did a tall column stop being worth its own height? Answer that, then put it away — nothing ahead of us needs it. What is ahead of us is a promise I made you back in the bowl, and where that promise runs out.

[grave] The country has changed character ahead of us. There is a ridge running clean across our track with an edge on it like a folded sheet of steel, and past that, something standing up with a point on it. I am taking the speed right off.

[gentle] Good. This stop exists because I have been telling you a comfortable story for half an hour and it is time I showed you where it stops being true. Helm, bring the plate in and set it down on the ridge, the same way we did back in the bowl.

[dry] Before it touches. That plate sat down on two needles in the bowl and it held like it was bolted. On a ridge with an edge like folded steel: does it sit, does it rock, or does it not come down at all? Choose. And keep your eye on the near edge of it.

[reflective] Plate coming down. It has touched — and it is rocking. Catching on the near side, tipping over, catching on the far side. It will not sit, Doc. There is nothing under there for it to lie flat against, and it has tried on its own four times.

[dry] Then put the sheets back up and take the needles off it, because that is precisely what fixed the plate the last time we had this argument. Two needles, one plate, and it settled straight away without a word of complaint. Do it again and let us all go home early.

[warm] Sheets up. And look at that — both curves are perfectly well behaved. Fore and aft, a smooth curve with a clean tangent on it. Port to starboard, another one. Two needles, no difficulty at all, exactly as it was in the bowl. Now look back at the plate.

[dry] Two good needles and a plate that will not sit down. Doc, then the needles were never enough. You stood there in the bowl and told us a point and two tilts fix the sheet completely, and I wrote it down. I would like that corrected, in front of everybody.

[grave] You are right, and I owe you it plainly. Two needles do fix a flat sheet — that part stands. What they do not do is promise the sheet is any use. Along the two directions I chose to look, this ridge is smooth. Along the direction it actually folds, it is a cliff, and both my cuts missed it.

[reflective] Inflating on the ridge as ordered. Six. And again. Doc, it is not opening out. The fold is exactly as sharp as it was when we arrived, and I can go closer if you want but I do not think it is going to help either of us.

[gentle] It will not, and that is the test that matters. In the bowl, zooming in flattened the ground and the film under the plate died away to nothing. Here it never does. Both slopes can exist and the surface can still be a cliff — smooth is more than having slopes. Say it back.

transitLines.text: [dry] Twelve stops on this run, and the one I am going to remember is the one where the plate would not sit down and Doc said so out loud instead of flying quietly past it. That is worth more to me than the nine stops where everything worked.

lines.text: [gentle] Before Helm climbs. The plate would not sit down on that ridge, and yet both needles were perfectly good. So what was it that the ridge did not have? One word will do, and it is not a word out of a book. Then we go up and look at the lot.

[hushed] All stations, end of the run. There are no walls to take down today — we lost those in the first four seconds — so I am simply going to climb, and keep climbing, until the whole country is in the window at once. Nobody talk over this one.

[hushed] There it is. All of it. The valley we came in along, the summit off to port, the pass with the ball still sitting in the middle of it, the fence with its kiss point marked, the column forest standing in one quarter, and the ridge scarring the far edge.

[reflective] It felt like a country for half an hour. From up here it is one sheet of hills, and we were crawling about on the surface of it the whole time, taking measurements a metre at a time. It never once occurred to me to ask how big the whole thing was.

[gentle] One sheet of hills, and one rule. Two numbers went in — where you are standing — and one came back out, how high it is. Everything we did today was a way of asking that single rule a question and getting an honest answer out of it.

[warm] Now look at the little map in the corner of your eye, the one that has been there since we boarded. Rings inside rings, a dot sitting on them, and a short arrow off the dot. That is a contour map, and it is this. You have been inside the diagram again.

[reflective] The arrow on that map is square to the rings. It has been square to the rings all afternoon, in the corner of my eye, and I never once looked at it properly until you told me what it was for.

[grave] Say the run back to yourself now, in the pieces you actually saw. Hold one direction still and the country is a curve. Two tilts hold a flat plate. The uphill arrow lies on the ground. Walk a ring and you never climb. Grow columns and add them up. Take your time over it.

[hushed] Thirteen stops. Helm logging the run complete, and for the record the walls stay down from here on. I am told there is no putting them back after a run like this one. Drive to standby, and the country holds where it is.

[gentle] They stay down. Say this one back and the whole country is yours: it was one rule, taking two numbers — where you stand — and handing back one, how high it is. Next time we cut the drive and let the field carry us. Thank you for flying.

fillers.text: [dry] Quiet stretch. Doc, I have spent a working lifetime reading contour maps on paper and treating the rings as decoration drawn around the bit I cared about. I would like the last twenty years back, in writing, at your earliest convenience.

[warm] Open ground either side and the rail is holding steady. If you want to look around, go ahead — the country is out there in every direction and it does not shift when you turn your head. That is the whole reason we took the walls down.

[gentle] One thing worth carrying between stops. Almost everything out here is the same move done twice: pick a direction, hold everything else still, and you are back to a single curve you already know perfectly well how to handle.

[dry] For the record, I have stopped asking whether the picture is cheating us. It has not cheated yet, and I have been watching for it fairly hard, which is more than I can say for how I sat through school.

[reflective] Long transit. Doc, does it ever bother you that we fly over about a millionth of a country like this one and then go home and call the thing understood? There is a great deal of ground out there that nobody on this ship has laid an instrument on.

[warm] Not in the least. You do not come to know a country by visiting all of it. You learn the rules it keeps, and then every part of it you land on afterwards is somewhere you have effectively already been.
